data.title: Apple working on AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding
data.description:
Apple is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms and others.

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one listing, Apple said it is seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel arrangements and prepare news briefings. There has also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software. 

Shares of Meta and Anthropic slid in late trading after Bloomberg News reported on Apple’s efforts. Meta fell nearly 2%, while Anthropic dropped more than 3%. 

Anthropic PBC recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc’s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk’s Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user’s behalf – in addition to offering standard AI agent features.

Apple’s App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No. 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Nov 19. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude were also in the top five.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor.

Bloomberg News reported earlier in November that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company’s plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as end-2027, but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the job listing reads. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

The listing says the company has a team building the “foundation for that future” and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to “make it real”. John Ternus, the tech giant’s new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI – with an agent being key to that effort.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same,” the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks” across apps, browsers, command lines, code and application programming interfaces, and they can “coordinate specialised subagents along the way”.

The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of “general-purpose computer-use agents”, the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Nov 19.

Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system’s design. “Agents that can run code, use credentials and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency.”

Sandboxing is a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet.

As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the upcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, it has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

With the change in 27.3, ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition. 

Apple has already been sued by the US Justice Department for actions such as blocking third-party access to features and hardware.

While Apple is still far from introducing its own full-fledged AI agent, it has taken steps to integrate its Siri digital assistant more deeply into third-party apps. The upcoming iOS 27.3 release lays the groundwork for deeper collaboration between Siri AI and outside applications, allowing the assistant to, say, book a car or restaurant reservation.

Still, the updated system doesn’t go as far as a full-fledged agent, which can autonomously carry out complex tasks across multiple apps and services in the background with little additional instruction from the user. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic soars 34% to US$2 trillion valuation on Wall Street debut
data.description:
NEW YORK - Anthropic shares soared more than 34% in their Nasdaq debut on Nov 19, pushing the AI giant’s value to about US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion) as investors shrugged off the Nvidia spy scandal and fears of a tech bubble.

The shares opened at US$111.50, up from the US$83 at which the company priced its shares on Nov 18, already above its expected range.

Anthropic raised a record US$81.3 billion, selling 980 million shares, about 956 million of them new shares and the rest from existing shareholders. The company itself will receive about US$79.4 billion.

The IPO’s original price valued the maker of the Claude chatbot at about US$1.5 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares.

The roughly US$2 trillion valuation at the open matches estimates floated earlier this year, before AI stocks slid on Wall Street.

The debut marks a milestone in the AI boom. A company founded five years ago by OpenAI defectors worried about AI safety has become the first of the leading model developers to list on Wall Street, at a valuation rivalling decades-old tech brands.

The listing, under the ticker “ANT,” gives ordinary investors their first chance to bet directly on a stand-alone AI giant.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” chief executive Dario Amodei said at the Nasdaq in New York’s Times Square, underlining the company’s priority of promoting safe AI.

‘Fresh air’

As is usual for large listings, the shares began trading well after the opening bell, once Nasdaq and the lead investment banks had gathered buy and sell orders to set an opening price.

The offering surpasses the US$75 billion that Elon Musk’s SpaceX raised in its June IPO at a valuation of US$1.77 trillion.

SpaceX’s total ultimately rose to US$86 billion after its underwriters exercised an option to buy additional shares. SpaceX shares opened 11% above their IPO price.

Anthropic has granted its underwriters an option to buy up to 147 million more shares, which would lift its total to about US$93.5 billion.

“Demand seems to be outstripping supply of this newly publicly traded company,” Art Hogan of B. Riley Wealth Management told AFP.

“This may be the breath of fresh air that the tech trade needed to move beyond the fog of artificial intelligence that we’ve been living in for the last couple of weeks,” he added.

The strong demand comes even as AI stocks have swung sharply, with investors questioning whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off.

Nvidia, the chip giant at the centre of the AI investment boom and an investor in Anthropic and dozens of other AI companies, has been shaken by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after a reported affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

Anthropic’s Claude models are among the most powerful in the world, hailed for their problem-solving potential but also feared for their capacity to destabilise societies and replace human workers.

The five-year-old company’s revenue has surged at a pace few US companies have ever matched, reaching US$17 billion in the third quarter, up from US$1.4 billion a year earlier.

Much of that revenue comes from customers paying to use its AI models for computer coding.

Amodei and his sister Daniela, the company’s president, founded Anthropic with several colleagues in 2021 after leaving ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.

Threats to Americans

Anthropic’s IPO filing goes into extensive detail on the risks of the technology, reflecting the company’s focus on safety even as it builds ever more powerful models.

It warns that advanced AI systems “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly.”

US Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren criticised the listing on X, saying the company “fails to answer for the potential threats to Americans’ retirements and the entire financial system if this IPO goes awry.”

About a dozen protesters gathered outside the Nasdaq on Nov 19, chanting: “Why you doing IPO? This AI bubble’s about to blow!” AFP

data.title: Alibaba’s AI ambitions face steep challenge in US chip controls
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding is facing mounting pressure to show it can deliver on its artificial intelligence business plan despite new limits on its access to data centre chips.

Its Hong Kong-listed shares capped a nine-day losing streak ahead of results due later on Nov 19 from the internet firm.

Alibaba’s market value stands at US$216 billion (S$278.43 billion), less than half its level just over a year ago, when investors were betting on it to lead China’s AI industry.

Draft US rules announced on Nov 16 would close a key workaround for Chinese hyperscalers to use advanced chips. That is making analysts turn more cautious on Chinese AI companies’ cloud growth potential, as well as their ability to train and run next-generation models.

“For Alibaba, they depend heavily on access to computing power, so this will be an important setback,” said Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak.

“It’s likely going to create a situation where it will take longer for them to build an ecosystem that can compete with the most advanced American technology.”

The new US rules are aimed at preventing Chinese firms from renting cutting-edge chips at data centres abroad.

Alibaba and its peers are already banned from direct-buying the most advanced processors, and Nvidia said this week it is no longer shipping lower-end Hopper data centre chips to China as well.

Part of Alibaba’s ambition to build 20GW of data centre capacity before 2032 depends on expansion across regions like South-east Asia. Chips made in-house by its T-Head unit may provide some buffer, but still trail the performance of Nvidia’s top products.

Fresh challenges aside, Alibaba’s results are expected to show a continued drag on its e-commerce business from sluggish Chinese consumption and tough competition.

Focus will be on whether that can be offset by its fast-growing cloud operation, which accounted for 18% of total revenue in the June quarter.

Among its peers, Tencent posted results after a Nov 18 close showing a negative profit impact from heavy AI spending. The company also warned that Washington’s curbs on Chinese access to overseas data centres will hamper development of its next AI model.

Nevertheless, JPMorgan Chase & Co analysts including Alex Yao expect US regulations to hurt Alibaba less than firms more directly exposed, like MiniMax Group.

“The rule covers China-headquartered cloud providers operating abroad, but we estimate AliCloud’s overseas AI revenue at below 10% of its cloud revenue, so the direct revenue impact is small,” they wrote in a note, maintaining overweight on Alibaba.

The bullish case is also bolstered by valuations, with the stock trading at about 10 times to forward earnings estimates. That is down from its three-year average of nearly 13 times and similar to current multiples for Tencent and Baidu.

Nomura Holdings analysts including Jialong Shi are cautious on the impact of the new regulations overall, though they see leading hyperscalers holding up better.

“Independent AI labs, perhaps with the exception of DeepSeek, could face greater challenges in securing advanced Nvidia GPU capacity to train their next-generation models,” they wrote in a note on Nov 17.

“Comparatively, Alibaba and ByteDance might be better positioned, in our view, supported by their existing GPU resources and greater financial capabilities.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic IPO raises US$81.3 billion to top SpaceX’s record debut
data.description:
Anthropic and its seven co-founders have raised US$81.3 billion (S$104.8 billion) in an upsized initial public offering, becoming the first frontier AI lab tapping the public markets to fund its development of thinking machines.

The artificial intelligence firm sold 956.4 million shares and the co-founders sold 23.6 million shares for US$83 each, according to a statement on Nov 18, above the marketed range.

The company had marketed 801.4 million shares, while the co-founders offered 23.6 million shares, in a range of US$70 to US$78 each, according to its filings.

Pricing the shares above the range gives the company a fully diluted valuation of roughly US$1.5 trillion.

The IPO is the biggest of all time, topping SpaceX’s US$75 billion base deal. Including a US$26 billion private placement listed in Anthropic’s filings, the offering as a whole would raise US$107.3 billion, lifting it above SpaceX’s total of US$86.2 billion including its so-called over-allotment option.

Anthropic’s debut marks a watershed moment for AI, signalling that investors have begun to expand their focus from primarily backing chipmakers and other infrastructure providers to the makers of platforms such as Claude, as they weave themselves into the fabric of business, academia, government and healthcare.

Soaring demand

Demand for the IPO soared, nearing seven times the number of orders for the shares available, Bloomberg News reported on Nov 15.

Buyers from Wall Street to London to Tokyo clamoured for a slice of a stock expected to quickly join indexes such as the Nasdaq 100 after it begins trading on Nov 19.

Bankers told prospective investors that existing backers would be prioritised by Anthropic, and some would-be buyers would receive smaller allocations than they expect, people familiar with the matter have said.

Some investors are offering a portion of their Anthropic IPO allocation to other prospective backers, letting them collect additional fees and reduce their risk before trading begins, while others with pre-IPO stakes are marketing them to buyers via special purpose vehicles.

At a roughly US$1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would join the 15 largest publicly traded companies, neck and neck with Tesla but ahead of Eli Lilly and Co, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The valuation is below the US$2 trillion floated months ago, but well above US$1.1 trillion that some on Wall Street suggested in the depths of the recent sell-off in tech stocks.

Anthropic’s listing is the first by a frontier AI lab, a cohort of firms building the most advanced models that are intended to tackle difficult problems and assist users in complex tasks such as software design, legal work and scientific discovery. The debut puts the company firmly ahead of rival OpenAI, which is not planning to go public before 2027.

The stock market did not offer a supportive setting for the Claude chatbot maker’s debut, with the Nasdaq 100 down 4.4% over the past week until closing on Nov 18.

Nvidia extended a losing streak to a fifth day, sinking 2.9% during regular trading, a day after the chipmaker reported earnings that beat expectations. It is set to buy US$10 billion of Anthropic stock as part of the private placement, the filings show.

“We’re not super fussed on when exactly, what month or what day, or what market conditions we go public into,” Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase & Co CEO Jamie Dimon at an event on Nov 13.

He said the best piece of advice he has received throughout the process is: “Never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it’s really worth.”

The debut is set to enhance the personal fortunes of the co-founders, including Amodei, as well as many of Anthropic’s employees.

It will also juice returns for its venture capital backers, including ICONIQ, Coatue Management and Spark Capital, which has a seat on the board.

Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley led Anthropic’s IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filing shows.

The stock is expected to trade on Nov 19 on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.
BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic’s US$1.5 trillion debut rewrites venture capital’s playbook
data.description:
For decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.

Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter cheques to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The AI lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Nov 19 at a US$1.5 trillion (S$1.94 trillion) valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies.

The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.

To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

Menlo, Spark reap big returns

Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple.

Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion.

Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board.

Writing the largest cheque in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5%, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.

To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.

Late-stage bets paid off

Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.

Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first cheque at the start of 2026, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.

It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2% of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue.

Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion in October, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May.

Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs.

The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4%.

“We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before,” said Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, which has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic.

“The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before.

“And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.” REUTERS

data.title: Why a woman overspends on her family even as she deals with a US$125k debt
data.description:
For many people, credit card debt can become like quicksand, especially when affordability is top of mind. For a year starting in October 2025, The New York Times followed four people who shared their lives, their spending habits, even their regrets, revealing a commonality: a mountain of debt.

This is the story of one of them, Adriana Dyurich, who aspires to build savings of US$18,000 (S$23,000) while trying to pay off a credit card debt of US$19,000 and a student loan of US$106,000.

data.title: Nvidia tells employees that company is moving on from Jensen Huang era
data.description:
SANTA CLARA – At a town-hall meeting with employees on Nov 18, Nvidia’s interim chief executive officer Colette Kress reiterated her confidence in the company after the ouster of long-time leader Jensen Huang.

“We’ve got this,” she told staff, repeating a phrase she used during the company’s earnings call the day before, according to a person who attended.

The chipmaker, facing external campaigns to reinstate Huang, also made it clear that the co-founder and CEO will not be coming back.

The meeting marked a new chapter for a company seeking to rebound from upheaval and scandal. Huang, who ran Nvidia for more than 30 years and built it into an AI powerhouse, left last week under the cloud of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman whom the US government has suspected of spying for China.

Flanked by more than 30 board members and senior executives, Kress touted the company’s recent financial results, thanking employees for their efforts in what she called a “great quarter”.

On Nov 17, the company topped analysts’ estimates with its sales and earnings and boosted its revenue forecast for the next fiscal year.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky spoke to the audience about the company’s core values, encouraging staff to remain intellectually honest and direct. 

The chipmaker’s roughly 47,300 employees are facing a future without the only CEO Nvidia has had. Under his leadership, they built a technology pioneer that’s central to the AI revolution. On Nov 18, Kress called them brilliant minds and said the mission would remain the same. 

Some current and former employees, as well as Silicon Valley figures close to Huang, are still supporting the old CEO and calling for his return. But the board has dismissed the idea.

The meeting ended with the Tom Petty and The Heartbreakers’ song I Won’t Back Down. BLOOMBERG

data.title: GTA 6 frenzy spotlights potential insurance risks lurking in digital infrastructure
data.description:
Millions of gamers around the world have logged on for the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, arguably the century’s most anticipated video game, offering a glimpse of the vast, interconnected digital infrastructure on which the global economy increasingly relies.

No major disruption is expected from the rollout. But the scale of demand around one of the gaming industry’s biggest releases underscores a broader risk for insurers: A failure at a shared cloud, payments or technology provider could affect thousands of businesses at once.

After 13 years in development and an estimated US$1 billion (S$1.29 billion) or more in production costs, Grand Theft Auto VI began rolling out globally on Nov 19, drawing the kind of attention that few entertainment releases command.

But the fervour also underscores how much modern businesses depend on the digital infrastructure that makes such mass online activity possible, and the risks insurers face when that infrastructure fails.

“A launch of the scale of GTA VI is effectively a built-in stress test of the shared digital economy infrastructure,” said Marcos Alvarez, managing director at Morningstar DBRS.

Insurers cover businesses against financial losses stemming from disruptions to their operations, including some caused by technology failures.

As companies increasingly rely on the same cloud providers, payment systems and digital platforms, a single outage could trigger claims from multiple policyholders at once, amplifying exposure.

Despite the frenzy surrounding the launch, any disruption on launch day or in the days that follow would not necessarily spell disaster for insurers, industry experts said.

“The recent technology outages have been a case in point with the gap between the economic cost and the actual insured loss being quite large due to policy limits, retentions, waiting periods, and coverage exclusions,” Alvarez added.

Business interruption could be a major source of claims, but coverage could also extend to costs associated with data recovery, system restoration, cyberattacks and outages at third-party technology providers, depending on the policy.

“This is an area that is evolving rapidly for the insurance industry. Insurers are refining how they assess, model and manage these interconnected exposures,” said Loretta Worters, a spokesperson for the Insurance Information Institute.

“That means looking beyond an individual company’s cybersecurity protections to understand its reliance on third-party providers, the concentration of those dependencies across their portfolios and the potential for a single event to generate losses across multiple policyholders.” REUTERS

data.title: Asian stocks fall, Anthropic slips in after-hours: Markets wrap
data.description:
TOKYO – Asian stocks sold off as pessimism over the artificial-intelligence trade hammered technology shares, with global equities set for their longest losing streak in three years. Anthropic fell in after-hours trading.

MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities index fell 1.7% – extending its decline to a seventh straight session – and poised for its lowest close since April. That pushed the MSCI All Country World Index – a key barometer of global stocks – on course for its longest losing streak since September 2023.

Anthropic, the maker of Claude, declined over 5% after hours to below US$92 (S$118.80), slipping beneath its lowest level during its stock-market debut on Nov 19. The shares had closed 17% above their IPO price even after Apple said it is developing its own AI agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic.

“Investors are questioning whether frontier AI is becoming a hugely successful technology but an increasingly difficult business in which to earn attractive returns,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets. “Apple’s reported move to develop its own AI agent only reinforces these concerns.”

Investors have retreated from one of the hottest corners of the market in 2026 as mounting doubts over the AI trade pressure technology stocks.

At the heart of the concern is whether returns from the boom will ultimately justify the vast sums being spent and borrowed to fund it, fuelling a broader decline in global equities.

“The Anthropic IPO has been a major success,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “However, the IPO does little to address the market’s bigger problems including AI profitability concerns, massive spending, higher interest rates, credit market stress and geopolitical risks.”

Elsewhere, emerging-market currencies slumped in US hours as a gauge of dollar strength hovered near its highest level since April 2025, the Bloomberg Commodity Index sank to its lowest since July and Treasuries rallied as investors sought haven assets.

Sentiment remained weak as futures for the S&P 500 Index dropped 0.3%, pointing to further losses for the US benchmark, which posted its longest slide since 2024.

Contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.6%, after the underlying gauge closed at its lowest level since April. 

“The initial euphoria around Anthropic’s listing is starting to fade a little, and that strong first-day performance isn’t translating into broader enthusiasm across the AI sector,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Beyond technology, oil prices swung amid concern that violence in the Middle East will re-escalate despite pressure on US President Donald Trump to pursue a diplomatic resolution to the nine-month war. 

The most-active contract for West Texas Intermediate traded near US$83 a barrel, after swinging in a range of more than US$2 in the previous session, and is down 5% for the week. Brent settled near US$92.

Gold fell and was heading for the biggest weekly decline since March, as hawkish Federal Reserve officials signalled more interest-rate hikes and a selloff in AI stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses.

Bullion dropped as much as 1% on Nov 20 to near US$3,590 an ounce, on track to lose more than 7% in a week that has seen the metal slide to the lowest since September 2025. Silver has lost around 13% in the same period. 

Meanwhile, Treasuries rallied, pushing yields lower across maturities, though the move offered only a reprieve from the broader pressure on the bond market. The 10-year yield, at around 5.02%, is poised to match its 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in a single year.

A stream of comments from Fed officials in recent days has reinforced expectations for further tightening. Traders expect the central bank to hike in December, followed by two more increases in 2027.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said he will consider all options when policymakers meet in December and did not push back against the possibility of a larger-than-usual rate increase.

“We’ve now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters on Nov 19.

“So everything’s always on the table, in my view, and how steep that path needs to be is determined by what we think is happening with inflation.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers
data.description:
Anthropic has made a superlative-filled debut on Wall Street, breaking all records for money raised on Wall Street as it became the first major artificial intelligence lab to become a publicly traded company.

The price tag on its shares was enough to put the value of the San Francisco company well beyond US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion).

That kind of number was once unheard of for a company’s first moments trading on the stock market. But an acceleration in corporate wealth – and most recently the AI boom – has changed that.

Anthropic is the second business to debut with a value over a trillion dollars, following SpaceX just months ago, and will join a handful of other tech giants that measure their wealth by figures reaching 13 digits.

Time will tell how Anthropic ultimately fares on the public market. The Claude maker decided to proceed with its IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, fears of a possible AI bubble and growing unease among the public about the technology’s risks overall.

Here are some numbers to help understand the IPO on Nov 19.

The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: US$81 billion

That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of trading on Nov 19, it offered 980 million shares priced at US$83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about US$75 billion in June.

The next biggest IPO hauls went to South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix US$26.5 billion in July and oil giant Saudi Aramco US$25.6 billion in 2019.

Anthropic’s initial valuation: US$1.5 trillion

The initial price per share was set at US$83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at US$111.50 a share – pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to US$2.01 trillion just before noon Eastern time (1am Singapore time on Nov 20).

By market close on Nov 19, Anthropic finished its first trading day at US$97.17 per share. That is still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly US$1.75 trillion.

In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of US$2.1 trillion. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion.

Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S&P 500: 11

Apple currently leads the pack at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they are not in the S&P 500 index yet.

Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over US$1 trillion. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018.

How far a trillion US dollar bills would stretch if laid end to end: 156 million kilometres

That would surpass the roughly 150 million kilometres between Earth and the sun.

The number “one trillion” is hard in itself for the human mind to comprehend. US$1 trillion is a thousand times greater than US$1 billion. And a million times more than US$1 million.

There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If US$1 trillion was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost US$122. AP

data.title: South Korea’s exports top US$1 trillion for first time on chip boom
data.description:
SEOUL – South Korea’s annual exports surpassed US$1 trillion (S$1.29 trillion) for the first time, making it the fourth country to reach the milestone after Germany, the US and China, and the first new entrant to the club in 19 years, as global spending on artificial intelligence sent semiconductor prices and shipments soaring.

Cumulative exports crossed the mark at 2.09pm on Nov 19, a year after first topping US$700 billion and 62 years after reaching US$100 million.

President Lee Jae Myung hailed the achievement as the culmination of generations of effort, paying tribute to workers who spent their youth in garment factories, shoe manufacturers and shipyards.

“The gains from exports must, above all, improve people’s lives,” he said in a message on X, pledging to ensure that growth benefits large and small companies and communities across the country.

“We must now turn this achievement into sustained growth. We will strengthen the competitiveness of our key industries and nurture future growth engines such as AI and biotechnology,” he said.

“We will also actively support Korean consumer products, including beauty products and food, as they expand into global markets.”

Germany and the US crossed the US$1 trillion mark in 2006, followed by China in 2007, riding a trade boom after China joined the World Trade Organization.

South Korea did so amid rising tariffs and the US-China rivalry, with a population of 51.6 million and an economy of just US$1.88 trillion, smaller than any of its predecessors at the time.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources projects full-year exports of US$1.17 trillion, up about 65% from a record US$709.3 billion in 2025.

“Given our smaller population and economy, this is a remarkable achievement,” Kang Kam-chan, the ministry’s deputy minister for trade and investment, told reporters.

Chips lead, but not alone

Exports totalled US$930.2 billion in the first 10 months, including US$396.8 billion in semiconductors, accounting for about 43% of the total and nearly triple the previous record for the period.

AI data centre demand drove up DRAM and NAND prices, while the build-out lifted shipments of solid-state drives, transformers, cables and copper, according to the ministry.

Exports excluding chips rose 20%, with 16 of 20 major categories gaining. Cosmetics exports reached US$12.4 billion, topping the 2025 full-year record in 10 months.

Shipments rose in seven of nine major markets, led by China, up 88%, and the US, up 77%.

Small and mid-sized companies also posted record exports.

Imports rose 21% to US$635.1 billion, leaving a surplus of about US$295 billion through October, against US$77.4 billion for all of 2025.

“Part of the US$1 trillion belongs to imports,” Kang said, citing steady supplies of crude oil, naphtha and chipmaking equipment.

Bigger numbers, thinner spread

Much of the record reflects higher prices, not higher output.

Kang said rising prices drove much of the growth, as AI demand sent memory chip prices soaring and petroleum product export prices jumped 62% to US$1,105 a tonne.

He acknowledged the gains have gone mostly to large companies, citing structural limits in chips and petrochemicals, which have short supply chains and employ relatively few workers, unlike automobiles or ships.

“It is regrettable that the profits have not flowed through to suppliers,” he said, adding that new chip plants and joint research with equipment makers could spread the benefits.

Normally, a large trade surplus lifts the won as exporters convert their dollar earnings into local currency. But many keep those dollars abroad or spend them on imported parts and overseas factories, meaning less of the surplus reaches the currency market.

From selling goods to investing abroad

Kang said exports could exceed US$1 trillion again in 2027, though easing chip and oil prices could pull them below the 2026 level.

He expects AI infrastructure demand to hold through the third quarter of 2027.

Delays in US data centre projects, Chinese competition and protectionism remain risks.

He said South Korea’s major industries appear to be undergoing a structural shift.

When exports first passed US$10 billion in 1977, they were led by ships, frozen fish, plywood and clothing.

The AI build-out now creates markets for South Korean power equipment, copper and aluminium alongside chips.

That shift, he said, calls for rethinking how South Korea manages its surpluses. Japan, Germany and China channelled theirs into overseas investments that now return income home.

“As an economy matures and costs rise, it cannot keep expanding production at home indefinitely,” Kang said. “The export structure has to gradually shift towards investment.”

He sees overseas investment as a way to build strategic ties, particularly with partners sensitive to trade deficits, such as the US, where the administration of Donald Trump has made shrinking them a priority.

South Korean factories abroad can create local jobs, buy from local suppliers and export to third markets, giving partners a stake in the relationship.

“Korea should not be a country that simply sells goods,” he said.

Asked whether South Korea would follow Japan, which came to rely on income from overseas investment after the 1985 Plaza Accord, Kang said his country is likely to take a similar path.

But he noted that Japanese companies prospered while ordinary Japanese saw fewer gains.

South Korea should instead keep research and “mother factories”, the advanced plants that develop new processes, at home while expanding overseas, he said.
THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

data.title: Easier QR code payments, smoother online checkouts to come with enhanced PayNow
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Consumers can look forward to easier QR code payments here and a smoother online shopping checkout process as enhancements to the PayNow instant payments system are rolled out progressively from 2027.

Tourists visiting Singapore and Singaporeans travelling overseas can also expect more payment options as links between local and regional QR payment networks are expanded through the enhanced SGQR+.

These proposed enhancements and their implementation road map were outlined in the PayNow Generation 2 Phase 2 report released by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) on Nov 18.

The first phase examined how PayNow has evolved since its 2017 launch, with findings released in June. The second phase has identified seven enhancements to address gaps identified in the review, to be made between 2027 and 2028.

Through the enhanced SGQR+, Singaporeans and tourists will be able to pay with their preferred apps without having to check which QR schemes are accepted by the merchant, as Singapore connects to more major regional QR networks through SGQR+.

This will also enable more Singapore merchants to accept payments from tourists through a wider pool of foreign payment networks and Singaporeans to pay through local apps in more countries.

Development of the SGQR+ switch, which will provide an additional connection between participating schemes rather than require merchants or payment providers to replace their existing arrangements, is already under way.

A limited roll-out in 2027 will connect an initial group of participating schemes and test live payment journeys before expanding in scope in 2028.

Another key enhancement is deep-linking. Already live in Lazada checkouts via the OCBC app, it seamlessly opens shoppers’ preferred payment app when they select PayNow when checking out on an e-commerce platform. This eliminates the need to screenshot or download QR codes and retrieve them in the payment app from their phone gallery.

Higher PayNow limits will also allow Singaporeans to make and receive larger government payments with instant confirmation. The enhancement will first be introduced in late 2027 with one government agency, which has not been identified, before being progressively rolled out to other agencies from 2028.

Singapore currently applies a $200,000 limit for PayNow, which constrains its use for some high-value payments, such as property down payment or full payments for cars, above this threshold.

Clearer and more consistent rules will also be developed to address payment disputes, refunds, fraud and scams that may arise from individuals’ PayNow transactions to merchants.

This could offer customers and merchants a more consistent dispute resolution experience, with clearer processes and potentially faster resolution in certain cases, particularly those involving technical issues.

Such safeguards will be introduced in stages over 2028 by the Singapore Payments Network (SPaN), which was set up in 2025 by MAS and ABS to oversee Singapore’s national and cross-border payment schemes.

MAS will bring together SPaN, Banking Computer Services and other key partners to innovate new payment capabilities for emerging use cases, including AI agent-initiated payments.

Industry participants, including ABS, banks and payment service providers, will also test ways to process very large numbers of frequent micro-payments more cheaply.

OCBC said it has already enabled PayNow deep-linking with platforms such as Lazada, Pinduoduo, AXS, Frasers Mall and AnyWheel, as well as government agencies like the CPF Board for a more seamless checkout experience.

UOB said it is working with industry partners to explore some of the capabilities envisioned under the plans to enhance PayNow Generation 2, including how deep-linking and account-to-account payments can be more seamlessly integrated into online shopping journeys.

data.title: Alibaba tops revenue estimates on AI cloud growth; profit up on investment gains
data.description:
Alibaba beat estimates for September-quarter revenue on Nov 19 as demand for its AI cloud services surged, while investment gains helped more than triple reported profit.

China’s biggest e-commerce company by market share said revenue from AI cloud and computing services jumped 53%, highlighting the growing payoff from heavy investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and products.

“This quarter, our business delivered strong growth in both revenue and earnings because of our strategic focus on AI + Cloud growth and profit sustainability in Alibaba E-commerce Group,” Chief Financial Officer Toby Xu said.

Excluding investment gains and other items, non-GAAP net income leapt 92% to 19.9 billion yuan (S$3.85 billion), helped by stronger profitability and narrowing losses in its quick-commerce business.

Alibaba’s shares are down about 40% this year, as investors worry about weak consumer demand in China and rising spending on AI and cloud infrastructure.

Free cash flow was an outflow of 34.47 billion yuan in the quarter, compared with an outflow of 21.84 billion yuan a year earlier. Alibaba said the increase reflected higher spending on cloud infrastructure, partly offset by lower losses at Taobao Instant Commerce and higher customer pre-payments for cloud services.

Capital expenditure rose 60% to 50.48 billion yuan.

Alibaba reported quarterly revenue of 271.52 billion yuan, ahead of analysts’ average estimate of 269.81 billion yuan, according to LSEG data.

AI cloud and computing services revenue totalled 60.97 billion yuan. Alibaba has sharply increased spending on AI infrastructure, proprietary models and applications, betting on the technology as a key growth driver.

Adjusted earnings per American Depositary Share were 8.10 yuan, below analysts’ expectations of 11.16 yuan.

In September, Alibaba unveiled plans to expand global data-centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 and said its next-generation Qwen 4 model was in training. Its chip-design unit T-Head, which confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing earlier in November, also unveiled a new AI processor scheduled for commercial release in early 2027.

Alibaba launched a US$10 billion (S$12.92 billion) share placement in August, saying the proceeds would fund computing infrastructure and AI data centres.

The company recently reorganised its businesses into four main units: e-commerce, AI cloud and computing services, AI model applications and other businesses. REUTERS

data.title: GTA VI promises Sony a windfall, but Japan plays by different rules
data.description:
TOKYO – The global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov 19 is expected to provide a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony, though the franchise remains a niche pursuit in its home market of Japan.

The long-awaited, open-world, crime action game from Take-Two Interactive’s Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world, and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play.

About three-quarters of the 17 million GTA VI units sold are on PlayStation, according to estimates from Sensor Tower, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft.

Shares in Sony, whose PlayStation 5 (PS5) console is in its seventh year on the market, were up almost 3% in Tokyo compared with flat trading in the benchmark index.

Analysts think the global enthusiasm is unlikely to reach a fever pitch in Japan, where Switch 2 maker Nintendo dominates the gaming device market, and consumers prefer anime-style titles to realistic, violent Western games.

“The current trends in Japan don’t really fit this kind of game,” said Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda.

Given worldwide demand, “there’s absolutely no need for this game to sell in Japan”, he said.

Earlier in 2026, Sony scored a major global success with the movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day. In Japan, however, it faced competition from breakout hit Chiikawa The Movie: The Secret Of Mermaid Island.

“A few of my friends bought GTA VI at midnight, but I’m in no hurry to as it’s only on PS5 and Xbox, and you can’t play multiplayer online yet,” said Sorataka Goto, 33, who was shopping in Tokyo’s Akihabara electronics district.

“If and when it’s on PC and you can play online, I’ll consider buying it,” added Goto, who bought the remake of The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time.

Nintendo has sold more than five million copies of the Switch 2 title, which was originally on the Nintendo 64, in the first four days since its launch earlier in November.

“I had the original as a child, and so was excited to try this version,” Goto said.

GTA VI hype reaches Japan

Gamers in Japan may struggle to fully understand the satirical elements of GTA VI, the references to the Florida lifestyle and Western memes, said Serkan Toto, founder of game industry consultancy Kantan Games.

Still, the worldwide hype for GTA VI is spilling over to Japan, and marketing in the country is unprecedented for a Western-made game, he said.

In Akihabara, a large poster featuring the lead characters, Lucia Caminos ​and Jason Duval, was plastered on the side of a building.

“GTA VI will not become a mega blockbuster in Japan, but it will do very, very well,” Toto said.

Analysts expect the release of GTA VI to soften the decline of PS5 hardware sales in 2026 and support growth in software sales.

Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July-September quarter, which analysts see as reflecting demand ahead of GTA VI, down from 4 million a year earlier.

“We’ve modelled PlayStation profits materially ahead of the Street in the next couple of quarters, on account of the GTA VI launch,” Bernstein analyst David Dai wrote in a note.

The release is bolstering Sony’s games slate after it delayed the launch of God Of War Laufey by three months to May 2027.

Sony is grappling with procurement challenges as the cost of memory chips has risen sharply due to the AI boom.

“I don’t get the sense that Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware. The benefits Sony gets from royalties will be enormous,” said Toyo Securities’ Yasuda. REUTERS

data.title: MindChamps founder seeks $86m for first pre-school fund to expand in Australia
data.description:
The founder of Singapore-listed MindChamps PreSchool has launched an investment platform that is seeking to raise A$100 million (S$86.4 million) for its first fund to acquire and develop purpose-built pre-school properties in Australia.

The platform, MindFunds, will pursue investments across the education sector, David Chiem, founder of MindChamps, a franchiser of pre-school centres, said in an interview.

The company has sold 45 franchise licences as part of its expansion in Australia, and the fund will acquire or develop properties where franchisees can open and operate their centres, he said.

MindChamps is targeting a first close for the fund in the first half of 2027, according to Goh Seh Harn, chief executive officer of Trigger Asset Management, who advises on the fund. It also plans a follow-on fund of A$500 million, he said.

Across Asia, growing demand for quality education has fuelled a rush of private capital into schools, opening up new sources of funding for a sector that has traditionally relied on equity and bank loans. Financiers such as Apollo Global Management and KKR & Co have bought stakes and lent money to school chains, betting that rising incomes and families’ willingness to spend more on their children will spur expansion.

MindChamps operates pre-schools, after-school care centres and therapy services for children. The Singapore-based company has also expanded into markets including Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Myanmar. BLOOMBERG

data.title: NETS pilots ‘tap QR to pay’; new app features make payments easier for tourists
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Consumers can soon use smartphones to complete purchases at NETS payment points – without scanning a QR code.

This was among the enhancements to the Nets App announced on Nov 18.

NETS is the first to pilot the tap QR facility to pay via SGQR.

This feature enables consumers to make payments simply by tapping their near-field communication-enabled smartphones at participating Nets SGQR points, without first opening the app.

It offers a convenient alternative to the existing scan-to-pay method.

This initiative, to run for two months, will be piloted in phases, starting in Toa Payoh in December. There are plans for a nationwide roll-out if the pilot is successful.

Tapping to pay via QR will initially be available through the Nets App, with support for other participating banking apps and wallets expected over time.

Nets group chief executive Lawrence Chan said: “As usage expands, our priority is to make QR payments more accessible for everyone, including visitors to Singapore, while advancing interoperability across the payments ecosystem.”

The other new features on the app will also benefit groups such as tourists, said the payment services group.

From now, those whose home-country payment apps are not linked to Singapore’s single, standardised QR code, or SGQR, can also use the local payment ecosystem through the Nets App.

Visitors from countries with established QR cross-border linkages with Singapore, such as China, India and Indonesia, can continue to pay directly through their local bank or wallet apps.

Other enhancements include a family wallet, through which users can use sub-wallets to support the spending needs of their dependants.

The primary user can set a spending limit and be notified of transactions in their sub-wallets. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Singapore-based DayOne to pause US IPO plans on data centre, market concerns: Sources
data.description:
SINGAPORE – DayOne Data Centers has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering (IPO) on hold, sources familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data centre operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion (S$6.46 billion) from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously.

But the company started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centres and AI stocks.

Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improves, the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.

The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup and BNP Paribas on the listing.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the sources said.

A representative for DayOne declined to comment.

Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets.

The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% in November, heading for its worst November performance since 2008.

Still, Anthropic staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement, and rose 17% on its trading debut on Nov 19, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.

Other data centre-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector.

In October, Firmus Grid abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever IPOs, while Blackstone-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027.

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data centre development, fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group.

The US in November put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data centre operators that they will need a licence to purchase American tech hardware.

DayOne’s backers include Coatue, Hillhouse, GDS Holdings, SoftBank Vision Fund and Citadel’s Ken Griffin. BLOOMBERG

data.title: ‘IPO and beyond’: GIC to stay invested in Anthropic following Nasdaq debut
data.description:
SINGAPORE – GIC intends to remain invested in artificial intelligence company Anthropic beyond its blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), as the Singapore sovereign wealth fund looks to deepen its partnership with the Claude chatbot maker.

Chris Emanuel, managing director and head of GIC’s Technology Investment Group, said in a LinkedIn post on Nov 20 that the fund was one of Anthropic’s largest investors, having participated in three funding rounds in less than a year.

“An IPO is an important milestone, but it’s just one moment in a company’s journey,” he said.

“We invest across multiple rounds, through the IPO and beyond. That’s life-cycle investing in practice.”

His comments came after Anthropic made the largest stock market debut on record on Nov 19, raising about US$81.3 billion (S$105 billion) through its IPO, which valued the company at around US$1.5 trillion at the offer price.

The American company priced its shares at US$83 apiece, above its initial range of US$70 to US$78, after increasing the size of its offering to 980 million shares amid strong investor demand.

Anthropic’s shares opened at US$111.50 on the Nasdaq, briefly lifting its valuation above US$2 trillion, before paring gains to close at US$97.17, up 17.1% from the IPO price.

Its strong debut contrasted with a broader Wall Street sell-off, as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell about 2.3% on Thursday amid concerns over elevated AI valuations and spending.

Beyond financial backing

Emanuel said GIC’s partnership with Anthropic extended beyond capital investment, with the fund drawing on its global network and investment platform to support the company’s expansion.

“Three rounds, three moves forward, in under a year. Today, GIC is one of Anthropic’s largest investors, and our partnership has grown well beyond the cheque,” he wrote.

The sovereign wealth fund has invested more than US$4.5 billion in Anthropic across its last three funding rounds, with its stake valued at about US$15 billion at the IPO price, Bloomberg reported.

The investments included Anthropic’s US$30 billion Series G funding round in February, which GIC co-led with US investment company Coatue. The round valued the AI company at US$380 billion.

Beyond financing, GIC has supported Anthropic’s AI infrastructure requirements through Theseus, connected its management with senior business leaders across the fund’s global network and assisted its international expansion, Emanuel said.

The fund has also invested in Ode, which helps enterprises deploy Anthropic’s technology.

Anthropic repeatedly stood out in conversations with customers, while its technical capabilities, mission and emphasis on developing AI responsibly strengthened the fund’s confidence in the company, he added.

“We build conviction, back it with scale over time, and bring the broader capabilities of GIC to the founders and companies we believe in,” said Emanuel.

Multibillion-dollar gains for investors

Anthropic’s listing has generated substantial paper gains for its early and late-stage backers, reflecting the rapid increase in the company’s valuation.

According to the Financial Times, Spark Capital, which invested in Anthropic when the company was valued at about US$4 billion in 2023, stood to hold roughly US$11 billion worth of shares at a US$1.4 trillion valuation.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested around US$3.2 billion, was estimated to hold a stake worth more than US$25 billion. Menlo Ventures’ investment of about US$1 billion was expected to be worth around US$21 billion.

Strategic investors Amazon and Google’s parent Alphabet collectively held close to 30% of Anthropic following the listing.

Anthropic’s rapid rise has been underpinned by strong demand for its AI models and enterprise services, although the company faces substantial computing and infrastructure costs as it expands.

Its annualised revenue reached about US$81 billion last month, up from roughly US$1 billion at the start of 2025, according to Reuters.

The company’s valuation has also climbed sharply, from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in its latest private-funding round in May 2026. THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: Don’t give AI agents your financial account login details, warns MAS chief Chia Der Jiun
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Consumers should avoid giving artificial intelligence agents their financial accounts’ login credentials as there are insufficient safeguards to ensure that such tools act safely and within their users’ instructions, said Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) managing director Chia Der Jiun.

Speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival on Nov 19, Chia noted that some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces into their offerings, but many financial institutions have yet to establish terms or channels for agents to access financial services.

“There are some challenges here,” he said. “The financial institution does not know if this is an agent that is acting on the full authorisation and control of the customer, nor whether the agent is transacting within its mandate and instructions.

“If agents transact incorrectly or beyond their instruction, who bears responsibility?”

Chia said a trusted protocol and a secure channel are needed for AI agents to access financial services, pointing to lessons learnt from the first phase of MAS’ Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) initiative.

These include ensuring that AI agents have sufficient autonomy to perform useful tasks while operating within clearly defined boundaries.

Their identities and authority to act on behalf of users must also be established, while their instructions should clearly specify what actions they can take, along with any limits and conditions.

“The greater the discretion and impact of action given an agent, the stronger the assurance and controls needed,” said Chia. 

MAS will also develop a common “know your agent” protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions.

The protocol, part of the new phase of SAFR, will provide financial institutions with information on the agent’s identity and whom it represents, what authority it has been given, what mandate it operates under, and its origins and reliability.

“This will allow financial institutions to determine the terms and scope permitted to an agent, and establish a dedicated secure channel for agent access,” said Chia. 

Separately, MAS will set up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute to bring together AI agents and programmable money, focusing on two use cases: corporate treasury management and payment services.

For corporate treasury management, banks could allow an AI agent to monitor a company’s liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds should move, and use tokenised deposits to execute permitted treasury actions.

Companies would set the mandates for their agents, while participating banks would set the controls and determine the terms for accepting each agent instruction.

For payment services, banks and payment service providers could allow customer agents to execute payment instructions using digital money, such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins.

Participating banks and payment service providers would verify the agents’ identities and authority, and apply risk controls before executing the transactions.

“The two use cases, and others that we will collaborate on in the future, would provide important lessons on the benefits and safeguards of such transactions,” said Chia.

“Consumers and businesses need to retain meaningful control over the objectives, mandate and actions of their agents.

“Autonomy has to be bounded. Actions and outcomes have to come with accountability,” he added.

MAS also announced on Nov 19 that it had successfully issued $100 million of tokenised MAS Bills on Nov 6.

The four-week MAS Bills were issued on the Singapore Dollar Test Network and settled using wholesale central bank digital currency, or CBDC.

Five primary dealers – DBS, HSBC, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB – participated in the issuance auction, with applications amounting to more than double the issuance size.

The tokenised MAS Bills will mature on Dec 4.

MAS said it intends to scale up tokenised MAS Bills issuances, bring on board more participating financial institutions and expand their use for collateral management.

Interested financial institutions and financial market infrastructure providers can be involved in the next phase of live trials in 2027, it added.

data.title: One app, many ways to pay: How DBS is shaping the next wave of digital payments with PayLah!
data.description:
For millions of Singaporeans, paying with DBS PayLah! has become part of their daily routines – from buying meals at hawker centres to paying at heartland shops and malls.

What began as a peer-to-peer mobile wallet more than a decade ago has grown into one of Singapore’s most widely used payment platforms, with over three million users.

DBS is now building on this foundation, extending the convenience of PayLah! beyond Singapore’s shores and into more payment situations. From shops across the Causeway to storefronts in China, PayLah! users can scan to pay just as they do at Singapore’s hawker centres – where PayLah! accounts for more than 60 per cent of QR transactions.

“The way people pay has evolved significantly over the past decade, and so have their expectations. Today, customers value not just the ability to pay digitally, but how simple and seamless the experience is,” said Chan Sow Han, head of Payments and Unsecured Lending at DBS Singapore.

“Our focus is to build on what customers already know and use, extending that ease of payment across more situations and locations so they can use PayLah! to pay wherever they are, while continuing to enhance the experience to better serve their needs.”

Making payments anywhere

QR payments are widely used across Asia, but payment systems and practices differ across markets. In China, for instance, customers may scan a merchant’s QR code or present their own for the cashier to scan.

DBS is addressing this through its latest expansion of PayLah!, which enables users to make QR payments at over 100 million participating Alipay+ and Weixin Pay merchants across China.

On top of existing UnionPay QR connectivity, DBS is the first and only bank in Singapore to support both payment methods across China’s three major QR payment ecosystems.

The development marks another milestone in DBS’ efforts to extend the payment habits Singaporeans are accustomed to at home across international borders. According to DBS, in 2022, it became the first bank in Singapore to enable consumers to make QR payments globally using a local app, through its partnership with UnionPay International.

Since then, PayLah!’s overseas reach has grown through partnerships with payment networks. These include DuitNow in Malaysia, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia, allowing customers to scan to pay when travelling to these destinations. This year, DBS said it also became the first Singapore bank to connect to Taiwan’s TWQR network, allowing PayLah! users to scan to pay at over 250,000 participating merchants in Taiwan.

“While QR payments are increasingly common across Asia, different markets have their own payment systems and ways of transacting. Our approach has been to work with established payment networks and partners to bridge these differences, so customers can enjoy a more consistent payment experience when travelling,” said Chan.

These efforts have translated into growing customer usage. Last year, PayLah!’s cross-border QR transaction volumes have grown 2.5 times year-on-year, while the number of unique users has doubled. Average spending per customer on PayLah!’s overseas QR transactions has also increased by approximately 30 per cent in the same period.

Recognising that customers have different payment preferences when travelling, DBS also introduced the TravelLah! Debit Card in September 2026, complementing PayLah!’s overseas QR payment capabilities with a debit card option.

Available to customers aged 16 and above, TravelLah! offers zero foreign exchange fees, using Visa exchange rates without additional mark-ups from DBS. Customers can pay in more than 150 currencies worldwide and view indicative exchange rates directly on the PayLah! app, giving them greater visibility over prevailing rates before they spend.

TravelLah! also offers zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency of overseas withdrawals.

The accompanying TravelLah! Debit Card Wallet within DBS PayLah! held in Singapore dollars can be topped up as needed, allowing customers to set aside funds for their travels without having to pre-convert or manage multiple currencies. Cardholders can also redeem complimentary basic travel insurance, subject to terms and conditions.

The card has attracted interest among younger customers, with around half of those who signed up in its first month aged between 16 and 29.

Designed for every stage of life

Beyond expanding where and how customers can pay, DBS is also enhancing PayLah! to better serve the needs of different customer groups.

“With a user base spanning different generations and life stages, we recognise that what customers expect from a payment app can vary considerably,” Chan explains. “A teenager learning to manage an allowance has different needs from a young adult travelling overseas or a senior who values simplicity when making digital payments.”

Rather than offering the same experience to everyone, DBS is moving towards a more personalised PayLah! experience, where customers can more easily access the features, offers and rewards most relevant to them.

For younger customers, DBS PayLah! for Teens, introduced in April 2026, offers an age-appropriate payment experience, including the ability to receive allowances digitally, customise transfer limits, and access relevant coupons and rewards. It also comes with built-in safeguards, including disabled auto-debit and spending controls, to help teenagers gain confidence in making digital payments safely.

A new senior-friendly mode was also launched last month, offering a simpler setup, with larger text, clearer navigation and easy access to core payment functions.

PayLah! also makes it easier for customers to get more value from their everyday spending. Those with DBS/POSB cards that earn DBS Points or POSB Daily$ can use their points to redeem a wide variety of rewards, including instantly offsetting eligible transactions, exchanging points for cash credits or Flexi eVouchers which can be used at NETS merchants across Singapore.

Beyond tailoring the experience to different users, DBS has also simplified everyday payment journeys, including online shopping through PayLah! Express Checkout. The feature enables customers to link their account once and subsequently complete purchases on participating platforms such as Lazada, foodpanda and Gojek. This allows customers to pay without switching between apps or entering card details on individual platforms.

Greater control and peace of mind

Backed by DBS, PayLah! combines the convenience of an everyday wallet with safeguards and customer controls that help customers manage their spending and transact with greater confidence.

To further safeguard customers, DBS will soon introduce complimentary wallet protection for all PayLah! users, providing coverage against unauthorised third-party transactions.

Looking ahead, DBS will continue expanding PayLah!’s payment capabilities while making the experience more personalised and rewarding.

“As we expand PayLah!’s capabilities, our focus is not simply on adding more features, but on making the experience more relevant to customers’ needs. We want them to derive greater value from each interaction, while retaining the simplicity and convenience they value,” said Chan.

data.title: US chip equipment maker KLA opens expanded site in Singapore, with plans for further growth
data.description:
SINGAPORE – US semiconductor equipment maker KLA opened an expanded plant in Singapore and announced it has plans for a third phase of expansion, making the Republic one of its major production hubs globally.

The expanded site, Building 22B in Ang Mo Kio, was announced in October 2024 and is now fully operational – giving the company about 210,000 sq ft of new operational space.

KLA, which makes machines and tools such as surface profilers, testers and semiconductor assembly solutions for chipmakers, established its presence in Singapore in 1996 and began manufacturing here in 2006.

Theo Kneepkens, KLA Singapore country president and senior vice-president of global operations, said the company has also outlined plans for a further expansion phase here, subject to finalisation of land arrangements and relevant approvals.

“I was actually hoping that this would already be a ground-breaking of our next phase. But we’re still defining a few details of our next phase of expansion before we can officially announce that,” he said.

“But it’s clear that our next phase of growth will be bigger than the current expanded site.”

Kneepkens said KLA’s plans for an additional phase reflect its conviction that Singapore – with its exceptional talent, supportive governance and strategic position – will remain indispensable in how the world manufactures critical semiconductor equipment powering AI and advanced computing.

In the longer term, Building 22B and the planned phase are expected to support about 1,000 new jobs across research and development, supply chain and manufacturing engineering.

KLA chief financial officer Bren Higgins said: “We’ve added hundreds of new roles, with over 2,200 employees working across multiple shifts, and 90% of KLA Singapore employees are locals, including both Singaporean citizens and permanent residents.”

He noted that KLA’s long-term investment in Singapore has been driven by the local talent, highly collaborative partners and access to suppliers and customers.

“We are experiencing unprecedented growth across the industry, and our customers show no signs of slowing. If anything, the demand environment is only accelerating,” he said.

KLA’s expansion comes on the heels of several investment commitments announced in the past few years by companies that fabricate semiconductors or are part of the manufacturing value chain, such as processors of silicon substrate materials and companies that test, assemble and package chips.

Chip firms that have made fresh investments include GlobalFoundries, Micron, Siltronic, Soitec, UMC, Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP Semiconductors.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said at KLA’s opening ceremony that Singapore has built a strong ecosystem for semiconductor equipment manufacturing, and the Republic now accounts for around one-fifth of global production.

“Singapore must keep building the specialised capabilities that companies need to compete.

“By working with partners like KLA, we can support their growth while creating good opportunities for our people and enterprises,” he said.

Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade), said that as chips become more powerful and specialised, manufacturing them requires greater precision.

Hence, equipment made by companies like KLA, which can measure process variations and detect defects early, is increasingly important.

“KLA is a key part of Singapore’s strength in this field. Its process-control tools help chipmakers bring advanced technologies into reliable, high-volume production,” he added.

He said Singapore is also investing in the research capabilities needed to seize new opportunities in the chip industry, committing $800 million under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 plan to the RIE Flagship in Semiconductors.

He lauded a three-year collaboration between KLA and A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics, saying such partnerships will help turn research into practical manufacturing solutions, so Singapore can continue to meet the semiconductor industry’s changing needs.

Local suppliers are evolving alongside the multinational companies they support, Gan added.

He cited precision engineering firm Sys-Mac Automation Engineering, which has strengthened its capabilities and shortened prototype development timelines in partnership with KLA.

Sys-Mac is also investing in new cleanroom capabilities to support KLA’s next-generation systems.

Gan added: “As our people and enterprises deepen their expertise, they can take on more demanding work and help companies like KLA grow from Singapore. And as KLA grows, it will in turn create more opportunities for our enterprises and people.”

Cindy Koh, executive vice-president at the Singapore Economic Development Board, said: “The opening of KLA’s latest manufacturing facility will deepen Singapore’s capabilities in semiconductor equipment development and create quality jobs for Singaporeans in manufacturing engineering and R&D, alongside training and upskilling opportunities.”

data.title: Alibaba defrauded shareholders by concealing ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal, lawsuit says
data.description:
NEW YORK – Alibaba was sued on Nov 19 in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.

Shareholders cited Alibaba’s relationship with Megaspeed, a ​Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia AI chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang.

The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14% over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of advanced processors.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant.

Nvidia faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.

Wu said on Nov 19 that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion (S$129 billion) in external cloud revenue and a 20% earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services in 2027. The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia.

In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the US Department of Defense linked to China’s military.
