In October, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to firms whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies. Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat as they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government.

The Nov 19 lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024, and Nov 11, 2026. REUTERS

data.title: ‘Almost all’ US Fed policymakers saw further interest rate hikes as likely, minutes show
data.description:
WASHINGTON – “Almost all” participants of the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate-setting meeting in October thought that further rate hikes would be necessary to fight stubbornly high inflation, minutes of the meeting showed on Nov 18.

The meeting’s minutes, released after a customary three-week lag, showed that according to almost all policymakers’ baseline outlooks for inflation and the labour market, further rate hikes “would likely be appropriate” to bring prices back under control.

The Fed held interest rates steady at its last meeting in late October, even as its chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation remained “too high”.

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75% and 4%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, had dissented in favour of an immediate 25-basis-point hike.

‘Broad-based’ inflation

The Fed has a dual mandate of keeping inflation to its long-term 2% target while ensuring maximum employment.

The unemployment rate in the US has been relatively steady over the last year, even as job growth has see-sawed. That stability is due to demographic changes and lower immigration.

Inflation, on a downward trajectory since hitting a pandemic peak, has reignited in the last year, driven by US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies and the energy price spike caused by his war on Iran.

The massive investments in infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence build-out have also led to increased prices.

Personal consumption expenditures price index inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, hit 3.6% in September, far above the central bank’s target.

At the meeting in October, participants “acknowledged that inflation remained elevated”.

“Most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad-based”, indicating they saw price increases as having spread beyond skyrocketing energy prices into other sectors.

Still, 10 of the committee’s 12 voting members called for rates to be held steady.

“These participants cited the need to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments,” the minutes said.

Those who dissented from the majority decision in calling for a 25-basis-point hike said they saw inflation as “too high” and “saw few signs of it abating”.

“They judged that the current policy stance was not sufficiently restrictive, and a few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later.”

‘Concerned’

Speaking to US broadcaster CNBC on the morning of Nov 18, before the minutes were released, Fed governor Christopher Waller said he was “very, very concerned” about inflation and now saw the need for a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” he said.

He said the Fed may need to go beyond the December rate hike he prescribed to meaningfully fight inflation.

Fed governor Michael Barr, speaking at an event in New York on Nov 18, also said he saw the need for further rate hikes. AFP

data.title: Tencent says new US chip curbs won’t hurt cloud revenue, may slow model training
data.description:
BEIJING – China’s Tencent Holdings said on Nov 18 that new US restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips would not substantially hurt its cloud revenue, though they would likely slow development of its next AI model.

Washington this week unveiled rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres.

Shares in Chinese cloud service providers, including Tencent, fell on Nov 17 after the announcement.

“We actually don’t see an impact, because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” chief strategy officer James Mitchell told analysts on a post-earnings call.

Mitchell said Tencent’s more efficient models could now be run on a “surprisingly limited number” of domestic chips.

“We think that our cloud revenue will not be substantially adversely affected by the changes,” he said.

President Martin Lau called the tighter restrictions “unfortunate” and said they left Chinese companies with less advanced computing power.

Lau said the measures would affect AI model training and likely slow development of Tencent’s next model in the near term.

Over the longer run, Chinese companies would have to rely on domestic supply chains and chips, he said, adding that the latest restrictions were likely to accelerate their development.

Missing expectations

The comments came after Tencent reported 8% growth in third-quarter revenue on Nov 18, missing expectations and slowing from the previous quarter as momentum in its gaming business cooled.

Demand for artificial intelligence services continued to boost Tencent’s cloud business, a key focus for investors assessing whether the company’s heavy AI spending is beginning to generate returns.

The tech giant reported revenue of 207.3 billion yuan (S$40.1 billion) for the three months ended September, below an LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan. Revenue grew 11% in the previous quarter.

Revenue from fintech and business services, which includes the cloud unit, rose 9% to 63.7 billion yuan, with demand for AI-related cloud services a key driver.

Chinese technology companies have struggled to secure advanced Nvidia chips because of longstanding US export restrictions, leaving them at a disadvantage to some US rivals.

Tencent said in 2025 that chip shortages were constraining cloud growth as it prioritised using AI chips internally over renting computing power to external clients.

Revenue from value-added services, which includes gaming, rose 3% to 98.3 billion yuan in the quarter.

Domestic gaming revenue increased 11%, while international gaming revenue slid 9%.

Net profit rose 0.8% to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analysts’ expectations of 59.46 billion yuan.

Capital expenditure totalled 81.4 billion yuan in the September quarter, up from 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter.

Tencent spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of 2026, exceeding the roughly 79 billion yuan it spent in all of 2025. REUTERS

data.title: Japan’s core inflation accelerates in October, cementing rate hike expectations
data.description:
TOKYO – Japan’s annual core inflation accelerated in October and exceeded the central bank’s 2% target for the second straight month, a sign of broadening price pressures that cements the case for a near-term interest rate hike.

The data will be among factors the Bank of Japan will scrutinise at its next two-day policy meeting ending on Dec 18, when many market players expect the central bank to raise its policy rate to 1.5% from the current 1.25%.

The core consumer price index (CPI), which strips away the effect of volatile fresh food, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier, data showed on Nov 20, compared with a median market forecast for a 2.3% gain. It followed a 2.1% rise in September.

An index that strips away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, rose 2.2% in October from a year earlier after increasing 2.4% in September.

Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, expects inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, to accelerate sharply over the coming months as firms continue to pass on rising raw material costs.

“The upshot is that we now expect the Bank of Japan to lift rates to 2.5% by the middle of next year,” he wrote in a research note.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September after delivering a hike in June – a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.

The central bank kept rates steady last month, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target. REUTERS

data.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower as Anthropic’s debut fails to revive AI fervour
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks slumped on Nov 19, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalise faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early spike in its share price ebbed.

All three major US stock indexes ended the session sharply lower, with the benchmark S&P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.

The S&P 500 was on course to post its steepest weekly loss since April 2025.

Anthropic’s debut, the largest IPO on record, was priced late on Nov 18 at US$83 per share and was widely viewed as the next high bar to clear for the AI trade.

The stock opened at US$111.50 shortly before noon.

After the company’s market valuation briefly surpassed US$2 trillion (S$2.5 trillion), its momentum began to lose steam.

“The Anthropic IPO is attracting gobs of attention,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St Louis, Missouri.

“That money is coming from somewhere; investors are making changes in their portfolio to incorporate Anthropic, so I wouldn’t extrapolate a whole lot of meaning from today’s trading behaviour, whether it’s up or down.”

Even so, Ellerbroek’s enthusiasm for the AI trade has waned.

“My beliefs about the growth in data centre capex spending have come down a little bit over the last month or two,” he added.

“Nvidia’s crisis situation is a big deal. The midterm elections have had an impact.”

“Data centres are going to be more expensive to build, and they’re going to be built more slowly.”

Advanced Micro Devices shares tumbled after investigative outlet Hunterbrook said its affiliated fund, Hunterbrook Capital, had taken a short position in the company.

Most chipmakers were lower, including Micron and Broadcom, among others.

Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed lower.

Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius sustained steep losses.

In other stocks, Palo Alto Networks shares jumped after the cybersecurity firm raised its 2027 revenue guidance.

Walmart dipped after the retail giant’s annual sales forecast disappointed investors.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.

Focus turns to the US Fed

Following the Nov 18 release of minutes from the US Federal Reserve’s October policy meeting, investors are recalibrating their expectations pertaining to upcoming rate decisions.

The minutes revealed a desire to rein in inflation even prior to the recent release of consumer and producer price indexes, which showed price pressures heating up.

Financial markets are currently pricing in about a 94% likelihood of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the central bank’s December meeting, with a small but growing chance of a super-sized 50-basis-point increase, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

Next week, the Commerce Department is expected to release its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, which includes the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index. Analysts expect the report to show year-on-year core inflation of 3.2%, well above the central bank’s 2% annual target. REUTERS

data.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
data.description:
NEW YORK - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Nov 19 that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

“There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” the spokesperson added.

Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions.

These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft’s global email outage, while in October crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.

After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said, adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents.

“Customers don’t distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here,” said Carissa Robb, of SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm.

“There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinising the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared,” Robb said.

A cyber extortion group called “n0n” claimed on Nov 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included “hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses,” according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.

The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review.

Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data.

JPMorgan declined to comment on the data.

The same hacking group on Nov 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data.

A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme. There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.”

The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review.

Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data.

Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data.

The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses.

The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. REUTERS

data.title: Australia’s jobless rate hits five-year high, markets ramp up rate-cut bets for 2027
data.description:
SYDNEY – Australian employment fell for a second straight month in October and the jobless rate climbed to a five-year high of 4.9%, a surprisingly soft result that bolstered the case that interest rates have peaked and the next move will be down.

Markets are no longer pricing in another Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) rate rise after five increases in 2026 took the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, and are pricing in lower rates in the second half of 2027.

The odds of a 25-basis-point rate cut at the RBA’s June 2027 meeting are seen at 68%, market pricing indicated, rising to about 90% for the August meeting.

By the end of 2027, around 45 basis points of easing are priced in, double what had been expected before the Nov 19 data.

That shift hit the already pressured Australian dollar, which was down 0.5% as it plumbed another 10-month low of 66.80 US cents. Three-year government bond futures rallied 15 ticks to 95.41, the highest since late August.

“With risks to both the RBA’s unemployment and inflation forecasts now skewed softer, we expect the bank to hold the cash rate at 4.85% until Q3 ’27, when it can begin moving back toward neutral,” analysts at Citi Australia said in a report.

“The risk for another hike still exists, but with the labour market weakening, we see the bar getting higher.”

Clear slowdown in labour market

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said employment fell by 43,500 in October from September, when it dropped a revised 36,400, the biggest two-month total for job losses in five years.

UBS, Nomura, the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and the National Australia Bank are all tipping a rate cut in August 2027, with stubbornly high inflation likely to keep the RBA on hold in the months ahead.

The fall in the number of employed in October 2026, which was driven mostly by part-time jobs, was well below analysts’ forecast for a rise of around 25,000.

The jobless rate climbed to 4.9%, the highest since October 2021, from 4.7% a month ago, reaching a level the RBA had not expected to see until the end of next year. Economists had expected a steady jobless rate.

“After months in which the impact of higher interest rates was most visible in housing, confidence and other interest rate-sensitive sectors, the slowdown is now showing up clearly in the labour market,” said Krishna Bhimavarapu, an economist at State Street Investment Management.

“Today’s report strengthens the case that policy is gaining traction, labour market rebalancing is under way and the hurdle for another near-term rate increase has risen materially.”

Anecdotal evidence of a broader rise in layoffs is building, and the RBA board members who voted against a hike earlier in November had flagged the risk that the economy was facing a sharper-than-expected downturn.

Retailer David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs after its collapse into administration, a union said on Nov 18, joining a string of job losses at Australian firms as the economy slows.

The latest jobs data also showed that the participation rate had dipped to 66.6%, from 66.8%, while hours worked fell 0.2%. Youth unemployment – for people aged 15 to 24 – rose to 11.3% in October, from 11.1%, the highest in five years. REUTERS

data.title: Oil prices gain as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns
data.description:
TOKYO – Oil prices edged higher on Nov 20, though set for a weekly decline, as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures rose 59 US cents, or 0.6%, to US$92.57 a barrel by 0720 GMT (3.20pm Singapore time). US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures for December climbed 42 US cents, or 0.5%, to US$83.63 a barrel, while the more-active January contract gained 60 US cents, or 0.7%, to US$83.04.

Both benchmarks settled little changed on Nov 19, but Brent is set for a 3.5% decline for the week while the December WTI contract is set for a 6% weekly drop, as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. Brent and WTI are set to fall for the third week in a row.

“Concerns over Middle Eastern crude oil supplies have resurfaced due to attacks on Riyadh by the Houthis, prompting buying,” said Satoru Yoshida, a commodity analyst at Rakuten Securities.

“Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support,” he said.

The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Iran-aligned movement.

Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and “exploded” and “are burning”, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Corps Navy in a statement carried by state media on Nov 19.

Iran’s intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the waterway, “running at roughly one incident per day in November”, still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to the global oil and gas trade, and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Nov 19.

However, some analysts were still expecting softness in the broader equity markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Nov 20 – heading for their worst week since 2020.

“Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices,” said Saxo analysts in a note.

In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Nov 18.

Separately on Nov 19, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would hit back hard after Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week and said he was dropping any idea of a moratorium on attacking energy sectors and shipping. REUTERS

data.title: High Court approves $391.9m collective sale of The Centrepoint’s leasehold rear block
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The High Court on Nov 19 gave the green light for a $391.9 million collective sale of the leasehold rear block of The Centrepoint.

This comes after The Straits Times reported on Nov 13 that a stop order had been issued by the Strata Titles Board (STB) in August, following two objections to the sale.

After the board issued the stop order, the collective sale committee applied to the High Court to seek approval for the sale of the seven-storey landmark property in Singapore’s prime shopping belt.

But the objecting owners – Tanxuan Investments, represented by law firm Drew & Napier, and an individual named in court records as Chin Yun Hee – withdrew their objections to the sale prior to the Nov 19 hearing before the High Court.

Citing confidentiality obligations, the lawyers for Tanxuan Investments declined to comment on what their client’s objections were about, or why these were withdrawn.

When asked on Nov 19, Frasers Property and marketing agent Savills Singapore did not specify the nature of the objections.

Observers say common objections include disputes over the apportionment of proceeds or collective sale price, or unit holders believing that the collective sale did not take place in good faith. 

The stop order for The Centrepoint’s collective sale is the only one issued so far in 2026, compared with one in 2025 for the $810 million collective sale of Thomson View condominium, an STB spokesperson said.

On Feb 26, Frasers Property, through its wholly owned subsidiary Frasers Property Cuppage, was awarded the $391.9 million collective sale tender for the leasehold rear block of The Centrepoint.

Based on the agreed apportionment method, retail unit owners each stand to receive proceeds ranging between $840,000 and $9.29 million. The apartment owners each stand to get between $2.65 million and $7.11 million per unit, subject to final adjustments.

This marks Savills Singapore’s fifth Orchard Road collective sale in recent years, with the combined transaction value totalling nearly $2.7 billion, said its managing director for investment sales and capital markets, Jeremy Lake.

Completed in 1983, The Centrepoint comprises two parts: a freehold front plot and a leasehold rear plot.

The leasehold rear block forms part of The Centrepoint at 176A Orchard Road, and comprises 66 retail units and 66 residential apartments. It occupies a prime site in Orchard Road with a direct sheltered link to Somerset MRT station.

The site has a land area of about 44,700 sq ft and is zoned “commercial”, with a gross plot ratio of 5.6 and a maximum height of up to 10 storeys.

Frasers Property said its acquisition of the site further strengthens its position in the Orchard Road area and its ability to maximise the potential of this well-located site.

Before the collective sale of the rear block, Frasers Property already held a majority stake in it, owning more than 52% of the units by strata area.

The developer is also the majority shareholder in the freehold front plot, owning about 96% of the units by strata area.

In addition, Frasers fully owns 51 Cuppage Road, a 10-storey office building connected to The Centrepoint.

A Frasers Property spokesperson said the acquisition of Cuppage Terrace and strengthened ownership of The Centrepoint’s rear plot “enhanced its Orchard Road precinct footprint”.

“This allows us to unlock synergies across adjacent sites, supporting the Government’s long-term masterplan to transform the precinct into a premier lifestyle destination. Our immediate focus remains on enhancing connectivity and visitor experiences across our assets,” the spokesperson said.

On Aug 31, Frasers Property announced its acquisition of Cuppage Terrace – a cluster of 17 conservation shophouses located next to The Centrepoint – for an agreed property value of $175 million.

Cuppage Terrace has a total gross floor area of 34,678 sq ft, excluding the outdoor refreshment area.

With the addition of Cuppage Terrace to its portfolio, Frasers wants to take a more coordinated approach to asset enhancement and long-term value creation.
